name: Algorithms
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: Searching, sorting, recursion, BFS and DFS, greedy choices and dynamic programming, with Python examples.

lesson.intro: An algorithm is a precise recipe for solving a problem. A handful of patterns, such as halving the search space, divide and conquer, exploring graphs and reusing answers to subproblems, solve a large share of the problems you will meet.

sections.title: Binary search and two pointers
sections.body:
Linear search checks items one by one. It works on any list and costs O(n).

Binary search needs a sorted list. It compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half that cannot contain it. Each step halves the range, so it takes O(log n) steps: about 20 for a million items. The loop runs while `lo <= hi`; once the range is empty, the target is not there. Python's `bisect` module does this for you.

Two pointers is another way to use sorted order. To find a pair that adds up to a target, start one index at each end. If the sum is too small, move the left index right to make it bigger; if it is too large, move the right index left. Each step rules out one item for good, so the scan is O(n) instead of checking all O(n^2) pairs.
sections.tip: Sorting first costs O(n log n). That pays off when you search many times, not for a single lookup.

check.question: At most, about how many comparisons does binary search need on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items?
check.explanation: Each step halves the range: 1,000,000, then 500,000, then 250,000, reaching a single item after about 20 halvings, because 2^20 is about a million. 500,000 is the average for linear search.

sections.title: Recursion and base cases
sections.body:
A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs two parts:

- A base case that returns directly without recursing.
- A recursive case that makes the input smaller, so it moves toward the base case.

If the base case is missing, or a call can skip past it, the calls never stop. Python raises `RecursionError` once the call depth passes its limit (1000 by default).

Each active call keeps its own stack frame with its own local variables until it returns, so a recursion n levels deep uses O(n) memory even if it creates no lists. When you write one, trust that the smaller call returns the right answer and only work out how to combine it with the current step.

check.question: What happens if you call factorial(5) after deleting its base case?
choices: It loops forever without using any memory
It recurses until Python raises RecursionError
check.explanation: Without a base case every call makes another call: 5, 4, ..., 0, -1 and onward. Each call adds a stack frame, and Python stops the program with RecursionError when the depth limit is reached.

sections.title: Sorting and stability
sections.body:
Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix: it takes the next item and shifts larger items right until the new one fits. It is O(n^2) in the worst case but close to O(n) on nearly sorted data, which makes it a good choice for small or almost sorted lists.

Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges the two sorted halves. It is always O(n log n) and needs O(n) extra memory.

Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the items into smaller and larger groups, and sorts each group recursively. It is O(n log n) on average and fast in practice, but bad pivots (for example, always the first item of an already sorted list) make it O(n^2).

A sort is stable if items with equal keys keep their original relative order. Insertion sort and merge sort are stable; typical quicksort is not. Stability lets you sort by several keys in passes. Python's `sorted` and `list.sort` use Timsort, which is stable and O(n log n).
sections.code:
def merge_sort(items):
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    mid = len(items) // 2
    left = merge_sort(items[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(items[mid:])
    merged, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:   # <= takes from the left on ties: stable
            merged.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    return merged + left[i:] + right[j:]

print(merge_sort([5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6]))   # [1, 2, 5, 5, 6, 9]

people = [("ana", 30), ("ben", 25), ("cy", 30)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))
# [('ben', 25), ('ana', 30), ('cy', 30)]  ana stays ahead of cy

check.question: Your list is already sorted. Which algorithm finishes in about n steps?
choices: Quicksort with the first item as pivot
None of them: sorting always takes n log n
check.explanation: Insertion sort compares each item with its left neighbor, sees it is already in place, and moves on: O(n). Merge sort still does O(n log n) work, and quicksort with a first-item pivot hits its O(n^2) worst case on sorted input.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.body:
Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph in layers: the start node, then every node one edge away, then two edges away, and so on. It uses a queue. Because it reaches nodes in order of distance, BFS finds the shortest path, counted in edges, in an unweighted graph.

Depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as far as it can, then backs up and tries the next branch. It uses a stack, often the call stack through recursion. DFS suits tasks such as visiting everything reachable, detecting cycles, solving mazes and ordering tasks by their dependencies.

Both must remember which nodes they have visited, or a cycle will send them around forever. With an adjacency list, both run in O(V + E) time: each vertex is visited once and each edge is examined once (twice if undirected).

check.question: You need the fewest moves between two squares on a grid where every move costs the same. Which traversal finds it directly?
choices: Either one: both find shortest paths
check.explanation: BFS reaches every square at distance 1 before any square at distance 2, so the first time it reaches the target it has used the fewest moves. DFS finds a path, but it may be a long, winding one.

sections.title: Greedy choices and dynamic programming
sections.body:
A greedy algorithm makes the choice that looks best right now and never revisits it. It is simple and fast, but only correct for problems where locally best choices add up to a globally best answer. Making change with coins of 25, 10, 5 and 1 works greedily. With coins of 1, 3 and 4, greedy pays 6 as 4 + 1 + 1, while 3 + 3 uses fewer coins.

Dynamic programming (DP) handles problems whose subproblems overlap. Instead of solving the same subproblem again and again, it solves each one once and stores the result. Top-down DP is recursion plus memoization: cache each result and look it up before recomputing. Bottom-up DP fills a table from the smallest subproblems upward.

Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values an exponential number of times. With memoization each fib(k) is computed once, so fib(n) takes O(n) time.

check.question: What makes a problem a good fit for dynamic programming?
choices: Every locally best choice is also globally best
The same subproblems come up again and again
check.explanation: DP saves work by solving each repeated subproblem once and reusing the answer. If locally best choices are always globally best, a simpler greedy algorithm is enough.

keyTerms.definition: Finds a target in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search range; O(log n).
A technique that moves two indexes through a sequence, often inward from both ends, to avoid nested loops.
The input for which a recursive function returns directly, without calling itself.
A sort that keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order.
A graph traversal that visits nodes in order of distance from the start, using a queue.
A graph traversal that follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack or recursion.
Caching the result of a function call so the same input is never computed twice.
An algorithm that takes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it.

summary: Binary search finds an item in O(log n) but only in sorted data; two pointers turn many O(n^2) pair searches into O(n).
Every recursive function needs a base case, and every call must move toward it.
Merge sort is O(n log n) and stable; quicksort is fast on average but O(n^2) with bad pivots; insertion sort suits small or nearly sorted lists.
BFS uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS uses a stack or recursion and goes deep first.
Greedy is fast but only sometimes correct; dynamic programming solves each overlapping subproblem once.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how you would find a name in a printed phone book, why that is much faster than reading every page, and why the trick stops working if the names are not in order.

questions.question: What must be true of a list before binary search can be used on it?
choices: Its length is a power of two
questions.explanation: Binary search decides which half to discard by comparing with the middle item, which only works if smaller items are on one side and larger ones on the other. Duplicates and any length are fine, and it works on any comparable items, such as strings.

questions.question: binary_search([2, 4, 6], 6) returns -1 even though 6 is in the list. What is the bug?
choices: The loop should run while lo <= hi; with lo < hi it never checks a one-item range
mid should be computed as (lo + hi) / 2
lo = mid + 1 should be lo = mid
The comparison items[mid] < target should use >
questions.explanation: After the first step lo and hi are both 2: a one-item range that holds 6. lo < hi is False, so the loop exits without looking at it. Using / gives a float that cannot index a list, and lo = mid can loop forever because the range stops shrinking.

questions.question: Fill the blank to complete this two-pointer palindrome check.
questions.explanation: After a matching pair, both pointers move inward: left goes right and right goes left, until they meet. right += 1 would move past the end of the string and raise IndexError.

questions.question: Two pointers moving inward from both ends find a pair with a given sum in a sorted list of n items. What is the worst-case time complexity? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Each step moves one pointer one place inward, and the scan stops when the pointers meet, so there are at most n - 1 steps. Checking every pair with nested loops would be O(n^2).

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: Starting at 5 and subtracting 2 gives 3, 1, -1, -3 and so on: n is never exactly 0, so the base case is skipped and the calls never stop. 9 is what you would get if the recursion stopped at 1. A safer base case is `if n <= 0`.

questions.question: This prints None instead of "done". Why?
choices: The base case should be n == 1
The recursive call's result is thrown away; it should be return count_down(n - 1)
questions.explanation: The base case does return "done", but only to the call one level up, which ignores it and falls off the end of the function, returning None. Every level must pass the result back with return.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: power(2, 5) is 2 * power(2, 4), which unfolds to 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * power(2, 0). The base case returns 1, so the result is 32.

questions.question: You sort a list of orders by date, then sort that result by customer with a stable sort. How are each customer's orders arranged?
questions.explanation: A stable sort keeps items with equal keys (the same customer) in the order they had going in, and going in they were sorted by date. This is how you sort by several keys with Python's sorted: sort by the minor key first, then by the major key.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: If every pivot is the smallest or largest item, as when the first item is the pivot of an already sorted list, each partition removes only one item: n + (n - 1) + ... + 1 steps. The average case is O(n log n), and random pivots make the worst case very unlikely.

questions.question: You need a sort that is guaranteed O(n log n) and stable, and extra memory is not a concern. Which fits?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case and keeps equal items in order. Heap sort is also guaranteed O(n log n) but is not stable. Quicksort can hit O(n^2), and insertion sort is O(n^2) in the worst case.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the list ends up in ascending order and the sort stays stable.
questions.explanation: Larger items shift right to make room. Using > stops at an equal item, so equal items keep their original order. >= still sorts, but it moves the new item ahead of equal ones, which breaks stability. < would sort in descending order.

questions.question: Which structure decides the order in which BFS visits nodes?
questions.explanation: BFS takes nodes from the front of a queue and adds new neighbors to the back, so nodes are processed in the order they were discovered, layer by layer. Swapping the queue for a stack turns it into a depth-first search. The set only tracks which nodes have been seen.

questions.question: Called as bfs("A"), this never returns. What is wrong?
choices: It never records visited nodes, so the cycle A, B, C, A keeps refilling the queue
BFS cannot run on directed graphs
order.append(node) should come after the for loop
questions.explanation: The graph has a cycle, and without a visited set every node is queued again each time it is reached. Adding a visited set and skipping nodes already in it fixes this. Changing popleft to pop turns it into a depth-first search, but it would still loop forever.

questions.question: With an adjacency list, what is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Each vertex is added to the queue and removed once, which is O(V), and each vertex's neighbor list is scanned once, which adds up to O(E) across the whole graph. DFS has the same cost.

questions.question: With coins of 1, 6 and 10, what does the greedy rule 'always take the largest coin that fits' do for an amount of 12?
choices: Fails, because 12 is not a multiple of 10
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 10 first and never reconsiders, leaving 2, which needs two 1s. It cannot see that skipping the 10 leads to a better total. Dynamic programming tries every coin for each amount and finds 6 + 6.

questions.question: Fill the blank to complete this memoized Fibonacci.
questions.explanation: If n is already cached, return the stored value instead of recomputing it. return fib(n) would call itself with the same n until RecursionError, and return memo would return the whole dict.

questions.question: What is the difference between a greedy algorithm and dynamic programming?
questions.answer: A greedy algorithm commits to the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it. Dynamic programming considers every option for each subproblem, stores each result, and builds the best overall answer from them.
questions.explanation: Greedy is faster and simpler but only correct for some problems; DP does more work but is correct whenever the problem breaks into overlapping subproblems.
